q: A team plans to roll the Datadog Agent out to a fleet that includes several legacy Linux distribution releases. What should they do before installing?
options: Nothing, because the Agent 7 package runs on every Linux release without issue
Confirm that each OS distribution and version is supported by the Agent version they plan to install
Install the Agent only on the newest hosts, because the Agent is supported on a single Linux distribution
explanation: Agent support depends on the operating system and its version, so compatibility must be checked against the supported platforms list before installing.
notes: Agent packages support specific OS distributions and versions, so not every release is supported.
Correct: the supported platforms tables list OS, version and Agent major version, so check them first.
The Agent supports many Linux distributions (Ubuntu, Debian, RHEL, SUSE, Amazon Linux and more).

q:
An engineer runs the following on a new host:

DD_API_KEY=<KEY> DD_SITE="datadoghq.eu" bash -c "$(curl -L https://install.datadoghq.com/scripts/install_script_agent7.sh)"

What does DD_SITE="datadoghq.eu" accomplish?
options: It configures the Agent to send its data to the EU1 Datadog site
It downloads the Agent package from an EU mirror but still sends data to US1
It adds a region:eu host tag while data still goes to the default site
explanation: DD_SITE sets the site option written to datadog.yaml, which determines the Datadog intake the Agent reports to; without it the default is datadoghq.com (US1).
notes: Correct: DD_SITE is written to the site setting, which selects the EU1 intake (datadoghq.eu).
The site setting controls where data is sent, not only where packages come from.
DD_SITE does not add tags; host tags are set with DD_TAGS or the tags option.

q: On a new Ansible control node, which command installs Datadog's recommended Ansible collection from Ansible Galaxy so its Agent role can be used in a playbook?
explanation: Datadog now recommends the datadog.dd collection, installed with ansible-galaxy collection install datadog.dd, and referenced as the datadog.dd.agent role. The standalone datadog.datadog role is legacy; pip install datadog installs the Python API client.
notes: Correct: datadog.dd is the recommended collection, installed with ansible-galaxy collection install.
ansible-playbook runs playbooks; it does not install roles or collections.
pip install datadog installs the Datadog Python API client, not Ansible content.

q:
This playbook uses the standalone datadog.datadog role. It installs the Agent, but the organization is hosted on the EU1 site and no data appears:

- hosts: servers
  roles:
    - { role: datadog.datadog, become: yes }
  vars:
    datadog_api_key: "<API_KEY>"

Which variable should be added under vars?
explanation: The role's datadog_site variable sets the intake site and defaults to datadoghq.com; an EU organization must set it to datadoghq.eu. Application keys are not used by the Agent.
notes: The hostname variable sets the host's name, not the Datadog site.
The Agent uses only the API key; application keys are for API read/manage access.
Correct: datadog_site defaults to datadoghq.com and must be datadoghq.eu for an EU1 org.

q: Which of the following is a configuration management tool that Datadog supports for deploying the Agent across many hosts?
explanation: Datadog provides integrations for deploying the Agent with configuration management tools such as Ansible, Chef, Puppet and SaltStack. Kibana and Nagios are visualization/monitoring tools, not deployment tools.
notes: Kibana is a visualization tool for Elasticsearch, not an Agent deployment tool.
Correct: Chef is listed with Ansible, Puppet, SaltStack and SCCM for deploying the Agent.
Nagios is a monitoring system; Datadog can ingest from it but does not deploy the Agent with it.

q: When starting the containerized Agent with docker run, which environment variable is REQUIRED?
explanation: DD_API_KEY has no default and is required; DD_SITE defaults to datadoghq.com and DD_HOSTNAME is autodetected.
notes: DD_SITE is optional and defaults to datadoghq.com.
DD_HOSTNAME is optional; the Agent autodetects the hostname.
Correct: DD_API_KEY has no default and is required to submit data.

q:
The standard docker run command for the Agent includes:

-v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock:ro

What is this mount for?
options: It exposes the Unix socket that application containers use to send DogStatsD custom metrics to the Agent
It gives the Agent access to the Docker API for container discovery and metrics
It persists the Agent's datadog.yaml and check configurations across container restarts
explanation: The Docker socket gives the Agent read access to the Docker API for container discovery, metadata and metrics. /proc and /sys/fs/cgroup are mounted for host and cgroup metrics.
notes: DogStatsD uses UDP 8125 or its own dsd socket, not the Docker daemon socket.
Correct: the Docker socket gives the Agent read access to the Docker API for discovery and metrics.
Configuration persistence uses other mounts; docker.sock is the Docker daemon API socket.

q: Which DD_TAGS value correctly assigns the two host tags env:prod and team:web to a containerized Agent?
explanation: DD_TAGS takes host tags separated by spaces, for example key1:value1 key2:value2.
notes: Semicolons are not a DD_TAGS separator.
Correct: DD_TAGS takes space-separated key:value host tags.
DD_TAGS is not a bracketed list with semicolons.

q: Application containers on the same Docker host send custom metrics to the Agent container, but none arrive. Which environment variable on the Agent container allows it to accept those packets?
explanation: DogStatsD only listens for local traffic by default; DD_DOGSTATSD_NON_LOCAL_TRAFFIC=true is required to receive metrics from other containers. DD_APM_NON_LOCAL_TRAFFIC does the same for traces on 8126, not metrics.
notes: Correct: DogStatsD listens only locally unless non-local traffic is allowed.
DD_APM_NON_LOCAL_TRAFFIC opens the trace receiver (8126), not DogStatsD.
DD_LOGS_ENABLED turns on log collection, not metric intake.

q: Which methods does Datadog provide for deploying the Agent on a Kubernetes cluster?
options: The Ansible Galaxy role run against each Kubernetes node
The one-line install script executed inside each application pod
The Datadog Helm chart or the Datadog Operator
explanation: Datadog supports installing the Agent on Kubernetes with the Datadog Operator, the Helm chart, or raw manifests, which deploy it as a DaemonSet on every node.
notes: Ansible deploys host Agents; Kubernetes uses the Operator, Helm or a DaemonSet manifest.
The install script is for hosts, not for running inside application pods.
Correct: the Datadog Operator (recommended) and Helm chart are the documented Kubernetes methods.

q: The Agent is installed directly on a Linux host (not in a container). The Docker check reports permission denied on /var/run/docker.sock. What is the recommended fix?
options: Change ownership of /etc/datadog-agent to root so that the Agent service runs with root privileges
Run usermod -a -G docker dd-agent, then restart the Agent
Set log_level: debug in datadog.yaml so the Docker check retries the socket with elevated permissions
explanation: The host Agent runs as the dd-agent user, which needs membership in the docker group to read the Docker socket.
notes: Making the Agent run as root is not the documented fix and is not best practice.
Correct: add dd-agent to the docker group so it can read the socket, then restart.
log_level only changes log verbosity; it does not grant permissions.

q: With the containerized Agent and default settings, which of these features is DISABLED until explicitly turned on?
options: Core host checks such as CPU and memory
explanation: DD_LOGS_ENABLED is disabled by default, while DD_APM_ENABLED defaults to true and core checks run by default.
notes: Correct: log collection is off by default and needs DD_LOGS_ENABLED=true.
DD_APM_ENABLED defaults to true, so traces are accepted by default.
Core checks such as CPU and memory run by default.

q: Which credential does the Datadog Agent require in order to submit metrics, events and logs to Datadog?
explanation: The API key is required by the Agent and for submitting data; application keys are used together with an API key for programmatic read/manage access.
notes: Application keys are for programmatic read/manage API access, not for the Agent.
Correct: the Agent requires an API key to submit data.
Client tokens are for browser and mobile apps (RUM, browser logs).

q: A frontend team wants to send browser logs and RUM data from a web application. Which credential should they embed in the JavaScript?
explanation: Client tokens are designed for browser and mobile apps; API keys must not be used client-side because they would be exposed to end users.
notes: Correct: client tokens are designed for browser, mobile and TV apps.
API keys would be exposed client-side, so they must not be embedded in browser code.
Application keys grant API read/manage access and must never be exposed.

q: An engineer created an API key used by 200 Agents and an application key used by a nightly reporting script. Their Datadog user is then disabled. What stops working?
options: Only the Agents, because the API key is revoked
Both, because all keys created by a disabled user are revoked
explanation: API keys belong to the organization and remain valid when their creator is disabled; application keys are tied to the user and are revoked when the user is disabled.
notes: API keys stay valid when their creator is disabled.
Correct: only the application key is revoked, so only the script breaks.
Only application keys are revoked; API keys created by the user remain valid.

q: An automation needs an application key that will keep working regardless of employee turnover. What is the recommended approach?
options: Create it under an admin user and transfer it to another admin when that person leaves
Skip the application key and call read endpoints with only the API key
Create the application key under a service account
explanation: Application keys are never transferred between users; service accounts are non-interactive accounts intended to own shared application keys.
notes: Datadog does not transfer application keys between users.
Read endpoints require an application key in addition to the API key.
Correct: service accounts are non-interactive accounts meant to own shared application keys.

q: By default, how many API keys can a Datadog organization have?
explanation: Organizations are limited to 50 API keys by default; Support can raise the limit if needed.
notes: 25 is not the default API key limit.
100 is not the default API key limit.
Correct: orgs get up to 50 API keys by default; Support can raise it.

q: An admin accidentally revokes the API key used by production Agents and notices two days later. What can be done?
options: Unrevoke it in the UI; API keys can be restored for 7 days
Nothing, since API key revocation is immediate and permanent
Ask Datadog Support to restore it, because revoked keys are retained for 30 days before deletion
explanation: A revoked API key stays listed as Revoked for 7 days and can be unrevoked during that window; application key revocation, by contrast, is permanent.
notes: Correct: revoked API keys stay listed for 7 days and can be unrevoked.
API key revocation can be undone within 7 days; application key revocation is permanent.
The restore window is 7 days in the UI, not 30 days via Support.

q: Which statement about revoking Datadog keys is correct?
options: Only revoked API keys can be restored (within 7 days)
Both API keys and application keys can be restored within 7 days of revocation
A revoked application key can be restored within 7 days, but API key revocation is permanent
explanation: The 7-day unrevoke window applies only to API keys; application key revocation is permanent.
notes: Correct: only API keys have the 7-day unrevoke window.
Application key revocation is permanent.
This is reversed: API keys can be restored, application keys cannot.

q: A script calls the Datadog API to query timeseries data. Which pair of HTTP headers must it send?
explanation: Read and manage endpoints such as GET /api/v1/query require both the API key (DD-API-KEY) and an application key (DD-APPLICATION-KEY); submitting metrics needs only the API key.
notes: Correct: read requests need both the API key and an application key.
An API key alone is enough to submit data, not to read it.
Client tokens are for browser/mobile data submission, not API queries.

q: Which request checks whether an API key is valid?
options: GET https://api.<site>/api/v1/query with the DD-API-KEY header
POST https://api.<site>/api/v2/series with an empty body
GET https://api.<site>/api/v1/validate with the DD-API-KEY header
explanation: The /api/v1/validate endpoint returns whether the supplied API key is valid. The query endpoint additionally requires an application key.
notes: The query endpoint also requires an application key, so it is not a key validation check.
The series endpoint submits metrics; it is not the validation endpoint.
Correct: GET /api/v1/validate checks the supplied API key.

q: A user creates an application key and does not assign any scopes. What can the key do?
options: Everything the creating user's permissions allow
Only read operations, until scopes are added
Nothing, until at least one scope is assigned
explanation: An unscoped application key inherits the permissions of the user (or service account) that owns it; scopes restrict it to a subset.
notes: Correct: an unscoped application key gets the creating user's permissions.
Unscoped keys are not limited to read-only access.
Unscoped keys are not disabled; they inherit the owner's permissions.

q: An API key was accidentally committed to a public Git repository. Which response follows Datadog's guidance?
options: Revoke it, scrub it from code and history, create and deploy a new key, then audit the account
Leave the key in place and do nothing further, because API keys can only submit data and cannot be abused by others
Rotate only the application keys, because an API key cannot be revoked while Agents are actively using it
explanation: Datadog's exposed-key procedure is revoke, scrub, create a new key, update affected services, and audit for unauthorized access.
notes: Correct: revoke, scrub, create a new key, update services, then audit the account.
Exposed API keys can be abused to send data, so they must be revoked and replaced.
API keys can be revoked at any time; the leaked key itself must be rotated.

q: How long is a newly created Datadog API key valid?
options: 90 days, after which it must be rotated
explanation: Datadog API and application keys have no automatic expiration, which is why storing them in a secrets manager and rotating them on exposure matters.
notes: Datadog keys have no 90-day expiry.
Datadog keys have no 1-year expiry.
Correct: API keys are long-lived with no built-in expiration.

q: On an Ubuntu host using systemd, the Agent was stopped to edit a check configuration. Which command brings it back up?
explanation: After a stop, the Agent service is started with systemctl start (or service datadog-agent start); restart is intended for an Agent that is already running.
notes: Correct: after a stop, systemctl start brings the Agent service back up.
datadog-agent has no restart subcommand; service control uses systemctl.
launch-gui opens the Agent Manager GUI; it does not start the service.

q: From an elevated PowerShell prompt on Windows, which command restarts the Agent service?
explanation: On Windows the Agent binary provides start-service, stopservice and restart-service to control the service through the service control manager.
notes: Correct: restart-service restarts the Agent through the Windows service control manager.
reload is not an Agent subcommand.
restart is not an agent.exe subcommand; the Windows form is restart-service.

q: Which agent.exe subcommand stops the Agent service on Windows?
explanation: The Windows-only service subcommands are start-service, restart-service and stopservice (no hyphen).
notes: stop-service is not the subcommand name; the stop command has no hyphen.
service-stop is not an Agent subcommand.
Correct: stopservice (no hyphen) stops the Agent service on Windows.

q: On a current macOS Agent installation (system-wide launchd service), which terminal command stops the Agent?
explanation: On macOS the Agent lifecycle is controlled with launchctl against system/com.datadoghq.agent (kill SIGTERM to stop, kickstart to start, kickstart -k to restart); systemctl and service are Linux service managers.
notes: Correct: launchctl kill SIGTERM on system/com.datadoghq.agent stops the macOS Agent.
systemctl is the Linux systemd service manager.
service is a Linux service wrapper, not used on macOS.

q: The Agent runs as a DaemonSet in Kubernetes. What is the documented way to restart the Agent on one node?
options: kubectl delete pod <AGENT_POD_NAME>, and the DaemonSet reschedules it
explanation: In Kubernetes the Agent pod is restarted by deleting it; the DaemonSet recreates it automatically. restart-service is Windows-only and containers do not use systemd.
notes: Agent containers do not run systemd.
restart-service is a Windows-only subcommand.
Correct: deleting the pod makes the DaemonSet reschedule it, which restarts the Agent.

q: What is the name of the Windows service that runs the main Datadog Agent?
explanation: On Windows the Agent runs as the DatadogAgent service, with separate services for the trace and process agents.
notes: dd-agent is the Linux user the Agent runs as.
datadog-agent is the Linux service and binary name.
Correct: the Windows service is DatadogAgent.

q: An Agent runs on an AWS EC2 instance whose OS hostname is the default ip-10-0-1-23. No hostname is configured in datadog.yaml. Which name does Datadog typically use as the canonical hostname?
options: ip-10-0-1-23, because the OS hostname always wins
The EC2 instance ID, such as i-0abc123def456
explanation: The Agent skips EC2 default hostnames (ip-..., domu...) when a better candidate exists; if the EC2 metadata endpoint is reachable it uses the instance ID. The DNS name is only a last resort.
notes: EC2 default hostnames such as ip-... are skipped when a better candidate exists.
The Agent does not use the private IP address as the hostname.
Correct: with metadata reachable, the EC2 instance ID is used.

q: Which datadog.yaml option overrides the hostname the Agent detects automatically?
explanation: Setting hostname in datadog.yaml (or DD_HOSTNAME in containers) defines the hostname the Agent reports.
notes: host_alias is not a datadog.yaml option; aliases are derived automatically.
display_name is not a datadog.yaml hostname option.
Correct: hostname (or DD_HOSTNAME) forces the Agent's reported hostname.

q: Which command prints the hostname that the running Agent reports to Datadog?
explanation: The hostname subcommand prints the hostname used by the Agent, which can differ from the OS hostname (for example, an EC2 instance ID).
notes: Correct: the hostname subcommand prints the hostname the Agent uses.
hostname -f prints the OS FQDN, which can differ from the Agent's hostname.
configcheck prints loaded check configurations, not the hostname.

q: A host is known as i-0abcd1234 (instance ID), ip-192-0-0-1 (internal hostname) and web01.corp.example (FQDN). How does Datadog represent this host?
options: Three separate hosts appear in the Infrastructure List, but only one of them is billed
One canonical name, with the others kept as host aliases
The shortest name is kept as the hostname and the other two names are discarded
explanation: When a host has several uniquely identifying names, Datadog picks a canonical name and submits the rest as aliases, visible in the Infrastructure List inspect panel.
notes: One host with several names is shown once, with aliases, not as three hosts.
Correct: Datadog chooses a canonical name and keeps the others as host aliases.
Other names are not discarded; they become aliases.

q: A containerized Agent 7.45 exits at startup with an error saying it cannot reliably determine the hostname. What resolves it?
options: Set DD_HOSTNAME, or let the Agent reach kubelet or cloud metadata
Set DD_TAGS="host:<name>" so that the hostname is taken from the host tag instead
Set DD_LOG_LEVEL=debug, which makes the Agent skip hostname validation at startup
explanation: Since Agent 7.40 the containerized Agent refuses to start without a reliable hostname; granting access to a provider or setting DD_HOSTNAME fixes it.
notes: Correct: set DD_HOSTNAME or give the Agent access to kubelet, the runtime or cloud metadata.
A host tag does not set the hostname.
Debug logging does not bypass hostname validation.

q: By default, how often does the Agent's collector run checks?
explanation: The collector gathers standard metrics every 15 seconds; 10 seconds is the DogStatsD flush interval.
notes: 10 seconds is the DogStatsD flush interval.
Correct: the collector gathers standard metrics every 15 seconds.
60 seconds is not the default collector interval.

q: Which statement about DogStatsD inside the Agent is correct?
options: It forwards every received point to Datadog immediately without aggregation
It aggregates received points and flushes them every 10 seconds
It runs checks from conf.d every 15 seconds
explanation: DogStatsD receives metrics over UDP (or a Unix socket) and aggregates each metric into one point per 10-second flush interval.
notes: DogStatsD aggregates points before sending.
Correct: DogStatsD aggregates each metric into one value per 10-second flush.
Running conf.d checks every 15 seconds is the collector's job.

q: Which Agent component sends the collected data to Datadog over HTTPS?
explanation: The collector runs checks, DogStatsD receives custom metrics, and the forwarder sends payloads to Datadog over HTTPS.
notes: Correct: the forwarder sends payloads to Datadog over HTTPS.
The collector runs checks; it hands data to the forwarder.
DogStatsD receives and aggregates custom metrics; it does not send to Datadog itself.

q: Which Agent component receives traces from tracing libraries on TCP port 8126?
explanation: The trace agent (APM agent) listens on 8126 for traces; the process agent collects live process data, and DogStatsD listens on UDP 8125.
notes: The process agent collects live process and container data.
Correct: the trace agent (APM receiver) listens on TCP 8126.
DogStatsD listens on UDP 8125.

q: Which Agent component executes the integration checks configured in conf.d?
explanation: The collector runs Agent checks (integrations and custom checks) and hands the results to the forwarder.
notes: Correct: the collector runs integration and custom checks.
The forwarder sends data to Datadog; it does not run checks.
The trace agent handles APM traces.

q: The network link from a host to Datadog is down for a while. What does the Agent forwarder do by default?
options: Writes all payloads to disk indefinitely until connectivity returns
Pauses the collector so that no new data is generated until connectivity returns
Buffers in memory up to a limit, then drops data
explanation: The forwarder retries from an in-memory queue bounded by forwarder_retry_queue_payloads_max_size; spilling to disk is optional and only enabled when forwarder_storage_max_size_in_bytes is set.
notes: Disk buffering is optional and off unless forwarder_storage_max_size_in_bytes is set.
The collector keeps running; the forwarder queues retries.
Correct: data is buffered in memory up to forwarder_retry_queue_payloads_max_size, then dropped.

q: Which Agent subcommand shows the overall state of the running Agent, including running checks, the forwarder, DogStatsD, logs and APM?
explanation: datadog-agent status prints a full status page for each component; health only gives a pass/fail readout.
notes: health only prints a pass/fail health readout.
Correct: status shows each component, including running checks, forwarder, DogStatsD, logs and APM.
version prints Agent version information only.

q: You want to run the nginx check once and see the metrics and service checks it produces. Which command does this?
explanation: The check subcommand runs a single check and prints its output; running it as dd-agent reproduces the Agent's permissions.
notes: configcheck lists loaded configurations; it does not run the check.
status shows the overall Agent state, not a single check run.
Correct: check runs one check and prints its metrics and service checks.

q: You added conf.d/postgres.d/conf.yaml but are unsure whether the running Agent loaded it and which values it resolved. Which subcommand shows this?
explanation: configcheck prints all configurations loaded and resolved by the running Agent, including Autodiscovery-resolved templates.
notes: diagnose runs connectivity diagnostics.
Correct: configcheck prints the loaded and resolved configurations.
flare packages logs and configs for Support.

q: Which Agent subcommand runs connectivity diagnostics?
explanation: diagnose runs connectivity diagnostics; health reports component health and hostname prints the hostname.
notes: health prints the Agent's component health.
hostname prints the hostname the Agent uses.
Correct: diagnose runs connectivity diagnostics.

q: What does the datadog-agent flare command do?
options: Restarts the Agent in debug mode for 15 minutes and uploads the resulting logs to the Log Explorer
Sends Support the Agent's logs and configs, with secrets scrubbed
Sends a test metric to Datadog to confirm the API key works
explanation: A flare bundles logs and configuration (with sensitive values scrubbed) and submits them to Datadog Support, optionally linked to a case.
notes: A flare does not send data to Log Explorer; it creates a Support archive.
Correct: a flare bundles logs and configs, scrubbing secrets, and sends them to Support.
A flare does not send test metrics; GET /api/v1/validate checks an API key.

q: Datadog Support asks you to attach a flare to case 1234567. Which command should you run?
explanation: Passing the case ID to the flare subcommand links the uploaded flare to that support case.
notes: status has no case option and does not upload anything.
Correct: flare <CASE_ID> attaches the flare to that support case.
diagnose runs connectivity checks and does not upload to a case.

q: The Agent runs in a Docker container named dd-agent. How do you view its status page?
explanation: Agent subcommands run inside the existing container with docker exec; docker run would start a new container.
notes: docker logs shows container output; it cannot run Agent subcommands.
Correct: docker exec runs the Agent's status inside the existing container.
docker run would start a new container instead of querying the running one.

q: How do you view the status of the Agent running in a Kubernetes pod?
explanation: Agent subcommands are run inside the Agent pod with kubectl exec; kubectl logs only shows container output.
notes: kubectl logs only prints container logs.
kubectl describe has no --status flag that runs the Agent status page.
Correct: kubectl exec runs agent status inside the Agent pod.

q: Which Agent subcommand prints the current health of the Agent?
explanation: health prints the Agent's current health; import converts configuration from older Agent versions.
notes: hostname prints the Agent's hostname.
Correct: health prints the Agent's current health.
import converts configuration from earlier Agent versions.

q: You want to watch, in real time, the log lines that the running Agent is processing to check a new log source. Which subcommand should you use?
explanation: stream-logs streams the logs processed by the running Agent, which helps verify log sources and processing rules.
notes: Correct: stream-logs streams logs processed by the running Agent.
check runs a single integration check.
flare sends logs and configs to Support.

q: Which Agent subcommand starts the Datadog Agent Manager GUI in a browser?
explanation: launch-gui opens the Agent GUI (port 5002), enabled by default on Windows and macOS.
notes: start-service is the Windows-only service start subcommand.
Correct: launch-gui starts the Datadog Agent Manager GUI.
config manages runtime configuration settings.

q: On Windows, where is the Agent binary that accepts subcommands such as status and flare?
explanation: The executable lives under %ProgramFiles%\Datadog\Datadog Agent\bin\; %ProgramData%\Datadog holds the configuration and logs.
notes: %ProgramData%\Datadog holds configuration and logs, not the binary.
The Agent is not installed into System32.
Correct: agent.exe is in %ProgramFiles%\Datadog\Datadog Agent\bin\.

q: What is the difference between the config and configcheck subcommands?
options: config validates the YAML syntax of datadog.yaml, while configcheck runs every configured check once and prints its output
They are aliases for the same command, kept for backward compatibility with Agent v5
config manages runtime settings; configcheck lists loaded check configs
explanation: config manages runtime settings (for example config set log_level debug), while configcheck lists the integration configurations the Agent loaded and resolved.
notes: config does not validate YAML, and configcheck does not run checks.
They are separate subcommands with different purposes.
Correct: config manages runtime settings; configcheck shows loaded and resolved check configs.

q: On Linux, in which directory are the Agent's log files written?
explanation: Linux Agent logs are under /var/log/datadog/. /opt/datadog-agent/logs is the macOS location (Agent 7.28+).
notes: /etc/datadog-agent holds configuration, not logs.
Correct: Linux Agent logs are in /var/log/datadog/.
/opt/datadog-agent/logs is the macOS log location (7.28+).

q: Where are the Agent log files on Windows?
explanation: Windows Agent logs are in C:\ProgramData\Datadog\logs (a hidden folder); Program Files holds the binaries.
notes: Program Files holds the Agent binaries.
Correct: Windows logs are in C:\ProgramData\Datadog\logs\.
C:\Windows\Logs is not used by the Agent.

q: On macOS with Agent 7.28 or later, where are the Agent log files?
explanation: macOS moved Agent logs to /opt/datadog-agent/logs in 7.28; /var/log/datadog was used by older macOS Agents and is the Linux location.
notes: /var/log/datadog was the macOS location before 7.28 and is the Linux location.
Correct: macOS Agent 7.28+ logs to /opt/datadog-agent/logs.
/Library/Logs/Datadog is not an Agent log location.

q: Traces from an instrumented service are not showing up in APM. Which Agent log file is the most relevant to inspect first on Linux?
explanation: The trace agent handles APM and writes to trace-agent.log; process-agent.log covers live processes and jmxfetch.log covers JMX checks.
notes: Correct: the trace agent handles APM and logs to trace-agent.log.
process-agent.log covers the process agent, not APM.
jmxfetch.log covers JMX-based checks.

q: You edited /etc/datadog-agent/datadog.yaml on an Ubuntu host where the Agent is already running as a systemd service. Which command is the documented way to restart the Agent so the change takes effect?
explanation: Ubuntu uses systemd, and the Linux Agent docs list sudo systemctl restart datadog-agent to restart the Agent service. restart-service is a Windows-only subcommand and launchctl is for macOS.
notes: restart-service is a Windows-only subcommand.
Correct: on systemd distributions such as Ubuntu, sudo systemctl restart datadog-agent restarts the Agent.
launchctl kickstart -k is the macOS restart command.

q: What is the default Agent log_level?
explanation: The default log_level is info; debug and trace are more verbose and are typically enabled only temporarily.
notes: warn is more restrictive than the default.
debug is more verbose and is enabled only temporarily.
Correct: the default log_level is info.

q:
datadog.yaml contains:

log_level: error

Which messages does agent.log record?
explanation: Each level includes the levels more severe than it, so error records error and critical messages.
notes: Each level also includes more severe levels, so CRITICAL is included too.
Correct: error logs error and critical messages.
WARN and INFO are less severe than error and are excluded.

q: Which log_level value produces the MOST verbose Agent logging?
explanation: The levels from least to most verbose are off, critical, error, warn, info, debug, trace; trace includes everything debug does and more.
notes: Correct: trace is the most verbose level.
debug is less verbose than trace.
info is the default and far less verbose.

q: With default settings, what happens when agent.log reaches 10 MB?
options: The Agent stops logging until it is restarted
It is compressed and uploaded to Datadog automatically
It is rolled over to agent.log.1, and only that one backup is kept
explanation: log_file_max_size defaults to 10 MB and log_file_max_rolls to 1, so one backup (agent.log.1) is kept and overwritten on the next rollover.
notes: The Agent keeps logging; it rolls the file over.
Logs are not uploaded automatically; rotation is local.
Correct: at 10 MB the file rolls to agent.log.1, with one backup kept by default.

q: How do you enable debug logging for a containerized Agent at startup?
explanation: Containerized Agents read their log level from DD_LOG_LEVEL; for Helm, logLevel in the values file sets it.
notes: Correct: DD_LOG_LEVEL=debug sets the containerized Agent's log level.
DD_DEBUG is not the Agent log-level variable.
Mount options do not change log verbosity.

q: The Linux Agent installer failed partway through. Where is the installer's log written?
options: ddagent-install.log in the current working directory
explanation: On Linux the install script writes ddagent-install.log to the current working directory; the Agent's runtime logs go to /var/log/datadog/.
notes: agent.log is the runtime log, not the installer log.
Correct: the Linux install script writes ddagent-install.log in the current directory.
/etc/datadog-agent holds configuration, not installer logs.

q: On Linux, where is the Agent's main configuration file?
explanation: Linux uses /etc/datadog-agent/datadog.yaml; /opt/datadog-agent/etc/datadog.yaml is the macOS path.
notes: /opt/datadog-agent/etc/datadog.yaml is the macOS path.
Correct: Linux uses /etc/datadog-agent/datadog.yaml.
/var/lib/datadog is not the config location.

q: On Windows, where is the Agent's datadog.yaml?
explanation: Windows configuration lives in %ProgramData%\Datadog, including datadog.yaml and the conf.d directory.
notes: Program Files holds binaries, not configuration.
Correct: datadog.yaml is in %ProgramData%\Datadog.
%AppData% is per-user and not used by the Agent.

q:
A Linux host shows:

$ ls /etc/datadog-agent/conf.d/redisdb.d/
auto_conf.yaml  conf.yaml.example

Redis runs directly on this host (no containers). What is the standard way to enable the Redis check?
options: Copy conf.yaml.example to conf.yaml, edit it, restart
Edit auto_conf.yaml with the connection settings, because it is picked up live with no restart needed
Add redisdb: true under the integrations section of datadog.yaml
explanation: conf.yaml.example is the template for each check; renaming or copying it to conf.yaml enables the check, and a restart applies it. auto_conf.yaml is for Autodiscovery.
notes: Correct: copy conf.yaml.example to conf.yaml, edit it and restart the Agent.
auto_conf.yaml is an Autodiscovery template for containers, not host config.
Integrations are not enabled with a flag in datadog.yaml.

q:
A host shows:

$ ls /etc/datadog-agent/conf.d/cpu.d/
conf.yaml.default

What is this file's role?
options: It enables the CPU check unless another config for it exists
It is an example template only and has no effect until it is renamed to conf.yaml
It holds global default settings that every other check in conf.d inherits
explanation: Files with a .default suffix enable core checks (CPU, memory, uptime, ...) out of the box; they're ignored when another configuration for that check is present.
notes: Correct: .default files enable core checks and are ignored if another config exists.
conf.yaml.example is the inactive template; .default files are active.
conf.yaml.default applies only to its own check, not to all checks.

q: A Redis container starts on a host running the containerized Agent and is monitored automatically without any user configuration. Which file in conf.d/redisdb.d/ makes this possible?
explanation: auto_conf.yaml files are Autodiscovery templates that apply the integration to matching containers automatically.
notes: conf.yaml.default enables core host checks such as CPU.
metrics.yaml lists default JMX beans for JMX checks.
Correct: auto_conf.yaml is the Autodiscovery template applied to matching containers.

q: In which kind of integration directory would you find a metrics.yaml file, and what does it contain?
options: In every check; it lists the custom metrics the check is billed for
In JMX-based checks; it lists the MBeans collected by default
In DogStatsD's directory; it maps StatsD metric types to Datadog types
explanation: metrics.yaml exists only in JMX checks and lists the default beans, so they don't have to be listed manually in labels or annotations.
notes: metrics.yaml is not a billing list and exists only in JMX checks.
Correct: JMX check folders include metrics.yaml listing beans collected by default.
DogStatsD has no metrics.yaml type mapping file.

q:
A custom check is not running. The files are:

/etc/datadog-agent/checks.d/disk_latency.py
/etc/datadog-agent/conf.d/disklatency.yaml

What is the most likely cause?
options: Custom check Python files must be placed in conf.d, not in checks.d
The YAML name must match the .py name
The configuration file must be named conf.yaml.default for custom checks
explanation: For a custom Agent check, checks.d/<name>.py and conf.d/<name>.yaml must use the same name, or the Agent won't pair the code with its configuration.
notes: checks.d is the correct place for custom check Python files.
Correct: the check file and its config file names must match.
Custom checks use <name>.yaml in conf.d, not conf.yaml.default.

q: You add a second instance to conf.d/nginx.d/conf.yaml while the Agent is running. When does the Agent start collecting from it?
options: Within one minute, when the Agent rescans conf.d
explanation: Changes to datadog.yaml and check configuration files take effect when the Agent next starts, so a restart is required.
notes: Checks do not pick up new config on their next run.
The Agent does not rescan conf.d every minute for static configs.
Correct: config file changes take effect after an Agent restart.

q: Where can you see every datadog.yaml option along with its default value?
options: In the output of the datadog-agent configcheck command
In the Running Checks section of the datadog-agent status output
explanation: The example datadog.yaml documents every option with its default, commented out; configcheck shows check configurations, not the full set of Agent defaults.
notes: configcheck shows check configurations, not every datadog.yaml option.
Correct: datadog.yaml.example lists every option with its default.
status shows runtime state, not configuration defaults.

q:
After this edit to datadog.yaml, APM is not configured as intended:

logs_enabled: true
apm_config:
enabled: true

What is the problem?
options: apm_config must be written on a single line as apm_config.enabled: true
enabled is not indented under apm_config
logs_enabled and apm_config cannot both be set in the same datadog.yaml file
explanation: YAML uses space indentation to define nesting; enabled must be indented under apm_config to belong to it. Datadog recommends validating config files with a YAML linter.
notes: Nested YAML is valid; dotted single-line keys are not required.
Correct: enabled must be indented under apm_config to be nested.
Both keys can coexist in the same datadog.yaml.

q: After a firewall change, a Linux host's Agent is running but no new data reaches Datadog. You want the Agent itself to test whether it can reach Datadog's endpoints. Which command should you run?
explanation: The diagnose subcommand runs the Agent's connectivity diagnostics against Datadog endpoints. health only reports whether Agent components are healthy, and configcheck lists loaded check configurations.
notes: health reports whether Agent components are healthy, not connectivity to Datadog.
Correct: diagnose runs connectivity diagnostics to Datadog.
configcheck lists loaded check configurations.

q: Which datadog.yaml block correctly sends the Agent's HTTPS traffic through proxy.corp.example:3128?
explanation: Proxy settings go under the proxy key with https, http and no_proxy children; https matters most because most Agent traffic is HTTPS.
notes: https_proxy is not a top-level datadog.yaml key.
Correct: the proxy block takes https, http and no_proxy children.
proxy_config is not a datadog.yaml option.

q: datadog.yaml sets proxy.https to http://proxy-a:3128, and the Agent's environment also sets DD_PROXY_HTTPS=http://proxy-b:3128. Which proxy does the Agent use for HTTPS?
options: Neither; conflicting settings make the Agent connect directly
explanation: For proxy settings, Datadog documents that environment variables (DD_PROXY_HTTPS, DD_PROXY_HTTP, DD_PROXY_NO_PROXY) override the datadog.yaml values.
notes: Correct: DD_* environment variables override datadog.yaml settings.
datadog.yaml loses when the matching environment variable is set.
The Agent does not fall back to a direct connection on conflict.

q: Which datadog.yaml setting must be true for the host Agent to collect logs?
explanation: logs_enabled: true turns on the Logs Agent; log_level only controls the Agent's own log verbosity.
notes: Correct: logs_enabled: true turns on log collection.
use_dogstatsd controls the DogStatsD server, not logs.
log_level controls the Agent's own log verbosity.

q: Which datadog.yaml snippet controls whether the Agent collects APM traces?
explanation: Trace collection is controlled by apm_config.enabled (DD_APM_ENABLED in containers), which defaults to true; process_config controls process collection.
notes: process_config controls process collection.
logs_config has no apm option; it configures log collection.
Correct: apm_config.enabled controls trace collection.

q: The http_check directory contains backend.yaml and frontend.yaml, both valid YAML with instances. How does the Agent treat them?
options: It loads only conf.yaml and ignores both files
Both files are loaded and all instances run
It loads whichever file is first alphabetically and ignores the other
explanation: The Agent loads every valid YAML file in conf.d/<check>.d/, letting you split a configuration across files. (The alphabetical rule applies only to duplicate log sources.)
notes: The Agent loads all valid YAML files in the check folder, not only conf.yaml.
Correct: every valid YAML file in conf.d/<check>.d/ is loaded.
Alphabetical precedence only applies to duplicate log sources.

q: The Agent was installed 15 minutes ago, but the host sends no data to Datadog. What should be checked FIRST?
options: Whether the latest Agent package is installed
Whether the host appears in the Host Map
explanation: The status output shows whether the API key is valid, which site the Agent uses and whether the forwarder is sending successfully, which covers the most common causes.
notes: Version checks come later; status shows the actual failure first.
Correct: status shows API key validity, site and forwarder errors.
The Host Map only shows the result, not why data is missing.

q: An organization is on the EU1 site. The Agent's API key is copied correctly, but datadog-agent status reports the API key as invalid. datadog.yaml has no site setting. What is the fix?
options: Generate an application key and add it to datadog.yaml
Set hostname to the EU region name
Set site: datadoghq.eu and restart the Agent
explanation: Without site, the Agent reports to datadoghq.com (US1), where an EU1 key is not valid. Each site is a separate instance, so the site must match the organization.
notes: The Agent does not use application keys.
hostname does not choose the Datadog site.
Correct: set site: datadoghq.eu (or DD_SITE) and restart.

q: An integration you configured does not appear at all under Running Checks in datadog-agent status. Which command best shows whether the Agent loaded its configuration?
explanation: configcheck lists every configuration the Agent loaded and resolved; if the check is missing, the file is misplaced, misnamed or invalid.
notes: health does not list loaded configurations.
Correct: configcheck shows whether the configuration was loaded and resolved.
version only prints version information.

q: datadog-agent status lists the mysql check under Running Checks with an error on instance #0. What is the best next step to see the detailed error?
options: Run sudo -u dd-agent -- datadog-agent check mysql
Delete conf.yaml.default from the mysql.d directory
explanation: Running the check manually as dd-agent prints its full output, including the error or traceback for the failing instance.
notes: Correct: running the check as dd-agent shows its full error output.
hostname is unrelated to a check's instance error.
Deleting a config file does not reveal why the instance is failing.

q: Graphs for one host show gaps and delayed points, and monitors trigger unexpectedly. The Clocks section of datadog-agent status shows a large NTP offset. What should be done?
options: Sync the host clock with NTP (outbound UDP 123)
Reduce min_collection_interval on every check so points are sent more often
Increase forwarder_retry_queue_payloads_max_size so delayed points are kept longer
explanation: Clock drift distorts metric timestamps; the fix is NTP synchronization, which needs outbound UDP 123.
notes: Correct: sync the clock with NTP; the Agent needs outbound UDP 123.
Collection frequency does not fix wrong timestamps.
A bigger retry queue does not correct clock drift.

q: The Agent should tail /var/log/myapp/app.log, but no logs arrive and the Agent reports permission denied. The file is owned by root with mode 600. What is the recommended fix?
options: Set log_level: debug so the Logs Agent retries the file with higher privileges
Grant the Agent user read access to the file and execute access to its directory
Set logs_enabled: false and back to true, then restart the Agent
explanation: The Agent does not run as root, so its user needs read permission on tailed files (and execute on the directories). Changing log_level or toggling logs_enabled does not change file permissions.
notes: log_level changes verbosity, not file permissions.
Correct: the Agent user needs read access to the file (and execute on its directories).
Toggling logs_enabled does not change file permissions.

q: The Agent fails with "Permission denied: '/var/log/datadog/...'" when writing its own logs. Which command fixes the ownership?
explanation: Agent log files and their directory must be owned by dd-agent; Datadog's fix is chown -R dd-agent:dd-agent /var/log/datadog/ followed by an Agent restart.
notes: chmod 777 on the config directory is insecure and does not fix log ownership.
Root ownership is the cause; logs must be owned by dd-agent.
Correct: chown -R dd-agent:dd-agent /var/log/datadog/, then restart.

q: datadog-agent status shows forwarder transactions failing with connection timeouts. A firewall sits between the host and the internet. Which outbound rule is most likely missing?
options: UDP 8125 to the Datadog intake endpoints
TCP 8126 to the Datadog intake endpoints
explanation: The Agent sends metrics, traces and logs over HTTPS on TCP 443. 8125 and 8126 are local ports for DogStatsD and APM on the host, not outbound destinations.
notes: 8125 UDP is the local DogStatsD port, not outbound to Datadog.
Correct: the Agent sends data to Datadog over HTTPS on TCP 443.
8126 is the local APM receiver port.

q: An engineer set logs_enabled: true in datadog.yaml and configured a log source an hour ago. Live Tail is empty, and datadog-agent status shows the Logs Agent is not running. What is the most likely cause?
options: Logs can only be collected by the containerized Agent
logs_enabled only takes effect after the next 15-second check run
The Agent was not restarted after datadog.yaml was edited
explanation: datadog.yaml changes apply only when the Agent next starts, so the Logs Agent stays off until a restart.
notes: Logs can be collected by host Agents too.
datadog.yaml settings are not applied on check runs.
Correct: datadog.yaml changes require an Agent restart.
